title: Prefer Header for HTTP
summary: Defines the Prefer HTTP header field, which a client uses to ask a server to behave in certain ways while handling a request. The server is free to ignore the preferences.

eli5.summary: A customer can say to a shop, if you can, please wrap it as a gift. The shop may or may not do so. This header lets a web client make such polite requests.

questions: how to ask a server for a preferred behavior
what does prefer return minimal do
subtitle: A polite HTTP request header for saying how you would like the server to behave, which the server may ignore.

tldr.problem: HTTP had no way for a client to state optional preferences about how a request is handled. The Expect header forces servers and intermediaries to reject unsupported expectations, and changing the URI can disturb caches.
tldr.mechanism: The Prefer request header lists preference tokens that a server is free to ignore, and an optional Preference-Applied response header says which were honored. The RFC defines respond-async, return, wait and handling, and an IANA registry for more.
tldr.outcome: Clients can ask for things like a minimal response or asynchronous handling without breaking servers that do not understand. The RFC has been updated by RFC 8144.

today: RFC 7240 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2014. It has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 8144.

sections.title: Why a Preference Header
sections.content:
A server or intermediary has many optional behaviors available while handling a request. For example, after a PUT the server may return the full modified resource or only a minimal acknowledgment. Returning the representation can save the client a follow-up GET. Servers also have to decide whether to tolerate a request that is technically invalid but understandable.

The decision belongs to the server, but it may want to defer to the client. HTTP offered no explicit way to do that. The Expect header does not fit: servers and intermediaries are required to reject requests with unrecognized or unsupported expectations, and every intermediary must process them. Query-string parameters alter the URI, which can have undesirable effects such as caches recording the altered URI.

This RFC therefore defines a new request header, Prefer, and a handful of initial preference tokens.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you want to ask a shop for a small favor, but not so strongly that they refuse you for not doing it. This header is that kind of favor.

sections.title: The Prefer Request Header
sections.content:
The Prefer header field says that particular server behaviors are preferred but not required for the request to succeed. It resembles Expect, except that servers are allowed to ignore the stated preferences. A server that does not recognize or cannot comply with a preference token MUST ignore it and continue processing rather than signaling an error.

Each preference is a token, optionally with a value and with parameters. Empty values are the same as no value. Token and parameter names are compared case-insensitively, while values are case sensitive. The order of parameters has no significance.

A client may send several Prefer header fields or one field with comma-separated tokens; the two forms are equivalent. A token SHOULD NOT appear more than once, and if it does, only the first instance counts.

The header is end to end, and a proxy MUST forward it unless it is marked hop by hop with Connection. A proxy that can honor a preference itself, such as respond-async using 202 (Accepted), may choose to do so. Implementers are told not to use Prefer for content negotiation. If a preference could change how a cache treats a response, the response MUST include Vary listing Prefer, or may use Vary: *, which makes the response uncacheable by a proxy.
sections.eli5: The client writes a short list of wishes on its request. The server reads the list and does what it can, and it never gets in trouble for skipping a wish.

sections.title: The Preference-Applied Response Header
sections.content:
A server may add a Preference-Applied header to a response to say which preference tokens it honored. Its syntax is like Prefer but without parameters.

The header is only needed when it is not readily apparent that a preference was applied and the ambiguity could affect how the client handles the response. With return=representation or return=minimal, for instance, the client may not be able to tell from the payload alone whether the preference was applied.
sections.eli5: After doing a favor, the shop can say "yes, I gift-wrapped it" so you know for sure.

sections.title: The Initial Preferences
sections.content:
respond-async says the client prefers an asynchronous response. If a response will take long, the server can reply with 202 (Accepted). How asynchronous handling works beyond that is implementation-specific and out of scope.

return=representation asks for the current state of the resource in the response to a successful request, saving a later GET. If the representation is of a different resource than the effective request URI, Content-Location can identify it. return=minimal asks for only a minimal response, typically 204 (No Content), which helps on limited-bandwidth mobile devices. The two are mutually exclusive, and a request with both can be treated as though neither were specified.

wait gives an upper bound, in seconds, that the client expects the server to take. If processing will take longer, the server or a proxy can respond asynchronously, for example with 202 (Accepted). Network and intermediary time add to what the client experiences, so a client with strict timing needs can adjust the value.

handling=strict asks the server to reject a request with recoverable errors using a 4xx response. handling=lenient asks it to try to process the request anyway. These two are also mutually exclusive.
sections.eli5: The first wishes are: "call me back later if this takes long", "send me the finished thing" or "just say it worked", "do not make me wait more than this long", and "be strict" or "be easygoing" about my mistakes.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The Prefer and Preference-Applied header fields were added to the "Permanent Message Header Field Names" registry. IANA also created an "HTTP Preferences" registry under the "Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Parameters" registry, with the Specification Required policy. Its initial contents are respond-async, return, wait and handling.

Requests go to the HTTP working group mailing list, and the Designated Expert approves or denies within at most 14 days. The expert checks, among other things, that the name and any values follow the ABNF, that the name suits the preference's specificity, that the preference does not constrain anyone to behavior required for successful processing, and that the defining specification discusses security considerations.
sections.eli5: There is a public list of known wishes. Someone checks new ones to make sure they are polite requests and not demands.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: A particular preference can introduce security concerns beyond those of HTTP/1.1, so implementers must consult each preference's own description. Complying can also cost a server more, for instance by providing a representation that would not ordinarily be sent or by committing resources to track state for an asynchronous response. Unconditional compliance could allow preferences to be used for denial of service. A server can simply ignore a preference to avoid committing resources.
sections.eli5: If the shop did every favor anyone asked, someone could ask for so many that the shop could never keep up. That is why saying no is allowed.

data.title: Asking for async handling after 10 seconds
data.code:
POST /collection HTTP/1.1
Host: example.org
Content-Type: text/plain
Prefer: respond-async, wait=10

{Data}
